modules.title: Pain, Injury, and Return to Training
modules.description: Evidence-based pain neuroscience, load management, tendinopathy rehabilitation, exercise regression, joint stress mapping, and return-to-training frameworks for coaching athletes through pain and injury.

evidence.title: Nociception Is Neither Sufficient Nor Necessary for Pain
evidence.summary: Nociception is the neural encoding of noxious stimuli via A-delta and C-fibers to the dorsal horn. Pain is a conscious, multisensory output generated by the CNS only when the brain concludes body tissues are in danger. The two are distinct physiological processes.
evidence.citation: Moseley GL, Butler DS. Explain Pain Supercharged (2017). NOI Group Publications.

evidence.title: Central Sensitization in Persistent Pain States
evidence.summary: In chronic conditions, CNS neural circuits become hyper-responsive, producing allodynia (pain from normally non-painful stimuli) and hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain from normally painful stimuli). Pain is then centrally maintained, not driven by active peripheral tissue injury.
evidence.citation: Woolf CJ. Central sensitization: implications for the diagnosis and treatment of pain. Pain (2011). PMID: 20961685.

evidence.title: The Fear-Avoidance Model of Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain
evidence.summary: Catastrophic misinterpretation of pain triggers kinesiophobia (fear of movement), leading to protective avoidance behaviors. Avoidance paradoxically maintains and amplifies threat beliefs, producing a vicious cycle of disuse syndrome, deconditioning, reduced tissue capacity, and worsened pain.
evidence.citation: Vlaeyen JWS, Linton SJ. Fear-avoidance model of chronic musculoskeletal pain: 12 years on. Pain (2012). PMID: 22463735.

evidence.title: Explain Pain: Pain Neuroscience Education Reduces Pain Catastrophizing
evidence.summary: Targeted pain neuroscience education (PNE) shifts understanding from a tissue-damage model to a CNS-protective-output model. Evidence shows PNE increases pain biology knowledge, decreases catastrophizing, and imparts short-term reductions in pain intensity and disability.
evidence.citation: Moseley GL, Butler DS. Fifteen years of Explain Pain. J Pain (2015). PMID: 26051220.

evidence.title: Weak Correlation Between Structural Imaging Findings and Pain
evidence.summary: Many asymptomatic individuals display bulging discs, rotator cuff tears, and meniscal degeneration on MRI. Epidemiological context added to imaging reports reduces threat perception and facilitates faster recovery by preventing catastrophic interpretation of normal age-related changes.
evidence.citation: Moseley GL, Karran EL. Contextualizing imaging findings reduces threat. Br J Sports Med (2020).

evidence.title: Catastrophic Coaching Language Induces Nocebo Effects
evidence.summary: Placebo and nocebo effects are mediated by opposite dopamine and endogenous opioid responses in brain reward circuits. Catastrophic language (e.g., 'your spine is crumbling', 'your shoulder is impinging') can biochemically amplify an athlete's pain experience through nocebo mechanisms.
evidence.citation: Colloca L, Barsky AJ. Placebo and nocebo effects. NEJM (2020). PMID: 32023380.

evidence.title: The Biopsychosocial Model in Sports Rehabilitation
evidence.summary: Modern rehab integrates biological tissue healing with psychological factors (pain catastrophizing, kinesiophobia, self-efficacy) and social factors (coaching environment, season timing, financial pressures). The isolated biomedical model is insufficient for complex pain presentations.
evidence.citation: Ardern CL, et al. 2016 Consensus Statement on Return to Sport. Br J Sports Med (2016). PMID: 26931321.

evidence.title: Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and the Training-Injury Paradox
evidence.summary: Athletes with high chronic workloads show lower injury risk than those with low chronic loads. Injury risk spikes when ACWR (acute 7-day load / chronic 28-day average) rises rapidly. Rehab is not cessation of training but controlled manipulation of ACWR to rebuild tissue tolerance.
evidence.citation: Gabbett TJ. The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? Br J Sports Med (2016). PMID: 26758673.

evidence.title: Progressive Loading Hierarchy for Tendinopathy Rehabilitation
evidence.summary: Tendinopathy rehab follows four phases: Phase 1 (Analgesia) heavy isometric holds for pain relief; Phase 2 (Strength) Heavy Slow Resistance with 3-4s eccentrics/concentrics for collagen synthesis; Phase 3 (Energy Storage) controlled plyometrics to retrain elastic energy; Phase 4 sport-specific return. Complete rest is contraindicated.
evidence.citation: Malliaras P, et al. Achilles and patellar tendinopathy loading programmes. Sports Med (2013). PMID: 23494406.

evidence.title: Isometric Analgesia for Tendon Pain Management
evidence.summary: Heavy isometric holds (e.g., Spanish squats, single-leg isometric leg press) induce immediate analgesia, reduce cortical inhibition, and preserve muscle bulk. Used in-season or during acute flare-ups to manage pain without irritating the tendon through repetitive loading.
evidence.citation: Rio E, et al. Isometric exercise induces analgesia and reduces inhibition in patellar tendinopathy. Br J Sports Med (2015). PMID: 25716183.

evidence.title: Exercise Regression Hierarchy: Load, Speed, ROM, Complexity, Vector
evidence.summary: When an athlete reports pain during an exercise, modify variables in priority order: (1) Load reduce absolute weight or volume; (2) Speed slow tempo (e.g., 3-1-3-0) to reduce peak forces; (3) Range of Motion restrict to pain-free joint angles; (4) Complexity switch bilateral to unilateral or dumbbell for free joint centration; (5) Movement Vector change angle to shift stress to different synergistic muscles.
evidence.citation: Reiman MP, et al. Exercise progression and regression in rehabilitation. Int J Sports Phys Ther (2014).

evidence.title: Graded Exposure and the Return to Sport Continuum
evidence.summary: RTS is a continuous process (not a single decision) spanning three stages: Return to Participation, Return to Sport, Return to Performance. The StARRT framework evaluates tissue health, psychological readiness, and social/contextual factors. Psychological readiness (fear of re-injury, self-efficacy) is often the primary barrier. Closed-skill testing (hop tests, dynamometry) must be supplemented with open-skill reactive agility and decision-making under fatigue before full clearance.
evidence.citation: Ardern CL, et al. 2016 Consensus Statement on Return to Sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy. Br J Sports Med (2016). PMID: 26931321.

evidence.title: Functional Movement Screen Has Limited Injury Prediction Validity
evidence.summary: Systematic reviews show FMS composite scores are poor predictors of future athletic injury. Injuries are complex, non-linear events driven by ACWR spikes, sleep deprivation, psychological stress, and contact dynamics none captured by a low-load movement screen. Use screening to individualize exercise prescription, not to pathologize movement strategies.
evidence.citation: Moran RW, et al. Do Functional Movement Screen composite scores predict injury? A systematic review with meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med (2017). PMID: 28446455.

evidence.title: Scope of Practice: Red Flags, Pain Severity Referral, and Non-Diagnostic Practice
evidence.summary: Coaches must not provide medical diagnoses. Clinical labels (Rotator Cuff Tendinitis, Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome) must be avoided; use functional movement constraints instead. Pain equal to or above 7 out of 10 during training or joint pain persisting more than 3 weeks despite pattern substitutions requires referral to a licensed physical therapist or physician. Serious pathology red flags (cauda equina, malignancy, infection, fracture) demand immediate medical referral.
evidence.citation: Finucane LM, et al. International Framework for Red Flags for Potential Serious Spinal Pathology. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther (2020). PMID: 32476330.

evidence.title: Unilateral Asymmetry Correction: 1.5x Volume for Lagging Limb
evidence.summary: If a user specifies limb strength asymmetry greater than 15 percent, assign 1.5x set volume to the lagging limb using unilateral movement variants, matching working loads to the capacity of the weaker side. Rehab accessory exercises are tracked separately and do not count toward hypertrophic MRV limits.
evidence.citation: Helm Engine Specification: Constraints and Safety Model (Section 6).

topics.title: Pain Neuroscience Fundamentals
topics.summary: Distinction between nociception (peripheral danger signaling) and pain (CNS protective output). Central sensitization produces allodynia and hyperalgesia in persistent pain states. The Explain Pain framework uses pain neuroscience education to reduce catastrophizing and threat perception.
topics.coachLens: Why does my shoulder still hurt even though the MRI looks fine?
topics.guidance: Teach the athlete that pain is a brain output reflecting perceived threat, not a direct measure of tissue damage. MRI findings in pain-free populations are common. Pain does not equal harm.

topics.title: Fear-Avoidance and Psychological Factors
topics.summary: The Fear-Avoidance Model explains how catastrophic pain interpretation triggers kinesiophobia and protective avoidance, leading to disuse syndrome and a vicious cycle of worsening pain. Catastrophic coaching language induces nocebo effects. The biopsychosocial model integrates psychological readiness and social context into rehab.
topics.coachLens: I'm afraid to overhead press because it might make my shoulder worse.
topics.guidance: Avoid catastrophic language. Normalize the athlete's experience while reframing it: pain during movement does not equal ongoing damage. Use graded exposure to reintroduce feared movements at tolerable loads. Explain that avoidance weakens the tissues that actually protect the joint.

topics.title: Load Management and Tissue Capacity
topics.summary: The training-injury prevention paradox: athletes with high chronic workloads have lower injury risk. Danger comes from acute spikes relative to chronic baseline (ACWR). Rehab rebuilds tissue capacity through controlled progressive loading, not rest. Complete rest reduces chronic workload base, creating re-injury risk on return.
topics.coachLens: Can I train through this pain? When is it safe to go heavy again?
topics.guidance: Training through pain is acceptable when pain stays at 3 to 4 out of 10 or less, subsides quickly post-session, and does not cause elevated next-morning pain. Never push through severe pain (7 or above out of 10). Rebuild load gradually using the exercise regression hierarchy, respecting the ACWR to avoid re-injury spikes. Return to heavy loads only after pain-free tolerance is established at submaximal intensities across full ROM.

topics.title: Tendinopathy Rehabilitation Protocol
topics.summary: Tendons respond to mechanical load via mechanotransduction. Complete rest is contraindicated. The progressive loading hierarchy: Phase 1 (Analgesia) heavy isometrics for pain relief; Phase 2 (Strength) Heavy Slow Resistance with 3-4s tempos; Phase 3 (Energy Storage) controlled plyometrics; Phase 4 sport-specific return. Isometric analgesia can be used in-season to manage acute tendon flare-ups.
topics.coachLens: My knee tendon hurts after squats. Should I just rest it?
topics.guidance: No complete rest degrades tendon capacity. Start with heavy isometric holds (e.g., Spanish squats, wall sits) to get pain relief while preserving muscle. Progress to Heavy Slow Resistance with 3-4 second eccentrics. Avoid fast stretch-shortening cycles until strength is symmetrical and morning-after pain is absent. Only then introduce plyometrics and return to sport loading.

topics.title: Exercise Regression and Movement Substitution
topics.summary: When pain limits an exercise, apply the regression hierarchy in order: (1) reduce Load/volume; (2) slow Speed/tempo; (3) restrict Range of Motion to pain-free angles; (4) reduce Complexity (bilateral to unilateral, barbell to dumbbell); (5) change Movement Vector to shift stress to different synergists. Goal is to maintain the highest possible training effect while keeping pain at 3 to 4 out of 10 or less.
topics.coachLens: My shoulder hurts on press what do I do?
topics.guidance: Don't stop training entirely. Start at step 1: reduce the weight. If pain persists at lighter load, slow the tempo (3-1-3-0). If still painful, restrict ROM (pin press from forehead height). If still painful, switch to unilateral dumbbell press with neutral grip. If still painful, change the vector entirely (overhead to incline or landmine press). Find the entry point where you can train without exceeding tolerable pain.

topics.title: Return to Training and Performance Frameworks
topics.summary: RTS is a continuum: Return to Participation, Return to Sport, Return to Performance. The StARRT framework balances tissue health, psychological readiness, and contextual factors. Psychological readiness (fear of re-injury) is often the primary barrier. Closed-skill tests (hop distance, dynamometry) must be supplemented with open-skill reactive agility under fatigue before full clearance. Graded exposure systematically reintroduces feared movements.
topics.coachLens: When is it safe to go heavy again?
topics.guidance: Progress through the return continuum: first achieve pain-free full ROM at submaximal loads, then rebuild strength symmetry, then introduce speed and energy-storage demands, then test open-skill reactive scenarios under fatigue. Use objective benchmarks (90 percent or above limb symmetry, pain-free morning-after) combined with psychological readiness scales. Don't clear based on a single closed-skill test.

topics.title: Scope of Practice, Screening, and Safety Boundaries
topics.summary: Coaches must not provide medical diagnoses use functional movement constraint labels, never clinical pathology terms. Refer when: pain is 7 out of 10 or above during training, or joint pain persists more than 3 weeks despite pattern substitutions. Movement screening tools (FMS) should individualize exercise prescription, not predict injury or pathologize movement. Limb asymmetry above 15 percent warrants 1.5x volume for the lagging limb matched to the weaker side's capacity. Be vigilant for serious pathology red flags: cauda equina, spinal malignancy, infection, fracture.
topics.coachLens: Is my form the reason I got injured? Should I get screened?
topics.guidance: Movement screening identifies baseline mobility and motor control patterns for exercise individualization it does not reliably predict future injury. Injuries result from complex interactions of load spikes, sleep, stress, and contact dynamics. Focus on progressive loading and capacity building rather than fixing perceived movement flaws. If pain is severe (7 out of 10 or above) or persistent (more than 3 weeks), refer to a physical therapist.

topics.title: Regional Joint Stress Mapping and Mandatory Substitutions
topics.summary: Specific pain presentations map to prohibited movement patterns and biomechanically safe engine substitutions. Subacromial impingement: avoid overhead pressing above 90 degrees abduction, substitute neutral-grip dumbbell press or landmine press. Patellar tendinopathy: avoid forward-translating knee squats, substitute Spanish squats or box squats with vertical shin vector. Flexion-intolerant lumbar: avoid bent-over barbell rows, substitute chest-supported rows or seated cable rows. Distal biceps tendinopathy: avoid straight-bar curls, substitute hammer curls or cable Bayesian curls.
topics.coachLens: My shoulder hurts on press what do I do?
topics.guidance: Map the pain to a movement constraint. For shoulder pain during overhead press: avoid deep dips and overhead pressing above 90 degrees abduction. Substitute with neutral-grip dumbbell press, low-incline cable fly, or landmine press. These preserve subacromial clearance space while allowing continued training of the pressing musculature.
